clinicalPearls: Dyshormonogenesis is a defect of thyroid hormone biosynthesis in a gland that is present and correctly located, distinguishing it from thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, ectopy or hypoplasia).
The gland is often goitrous because persistent thyroid-stimulating hormone drive causes glandular hyperplasia.
Most subtypes are autosomal recessive, so recurrence risk in siblings is higher than in sporadic dysgenesis and genetic counselling is important.
Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) deficiency is the commonest form and causes a total iodide organification defect with a positive perchlorate discharge test.
Pendred syndrome (SLC26A4/pendrin) combines dyshormonogenetic goitre with sensorineural hearing loss and a partial organification defect.
Defects in the hydrogen peroxide-generating system (DUOX2, DUOXA2) may cause transient rather than permanent congenital hypothyroidism, warranting later re-evaluation.
Serum thyroglobulin helps localise the defect, being low in thyroglobulin synthesis defects and preserved or high in other subtypes.
Prompt and adequate levothyroxine replacement prevents the irreversible neurodevelopmental damage of untreated congenital hypothyroidism.
reference.pathophysiology: Dyshormonogenesis encompasses inherited defects at successive steps of thyroid hormone synthesis within a structurally present, eutopic gland. Iodide must first be concentrated by the sodium-iodide symporter (SLC5A5); defects here impair trapping. Iodide is then transported at the apical membrane, partly via pendrin (SLC26A4), and organified onto thyroglobulin (TG) tyrosine residues by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) using hydrogen peroxide generated by the dual oxidase system (DUOX2 with its maturation factor DUOXA2). Iodinated tyrosines are coupled to form thyroid hormones, and iodine is recycled from mono- and di-iodotyrosines by iodotyrosine deiodinase (IYD/DEHAL1). A block at any step reduces hormone output; the resulting fall in circulating thyroid hormone releases the pituitary from negative feedback, driving sustained thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion that produces goitrous hyperplasia. Organification defects can be demonstrated by discharge of trapped iodide after perchlorate. The functional consequence is congenital hypothyroidism which, if uncorrected during the critical period of brain development, causes permanent cognitive and motor impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis, ectopic or hypoplastic gland)
Transient congenital hypothyroidism from maternal antithyroid drugs or iodine deficiency or excess
Transient hypothyroidism from maternal thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor blocking antibodies
Central (secondary) hypothyroidism from pituitary or hypothalamic disease
Thyroid hormone resistance or transport defects
additionalInvestigations: Newborn screening thyroid-stimulating hormone with confirmatory free thyroxine
Thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake scan to confirm a gland in situ
Perchlorate discharge test to identify organification defects
Serum thyroglobulin to distinguish thyroglobulin synthesis defects
Audiological assessment where Pendred syndrome is suspected
Targeted genetic testing of dyshormonogenesis genes and knee radiography to assess skeletal maturation
redFlags: Severe untreated hypothyroidism with lethargy, feeding failure and prolonged jaundice in the neonate
A large goitre causing airway or feeding compromise
Signs of evolving developmental delay indicating delayed or inadequate treatment
Coexisting sensorineural hearing loss suggesting Pendred syndrome requiring intervention
reference.prognosis: With early detection through newborn screening and prompt adequate levothyroxine, neurodevelopmental outcome is normal or near-normal. Delayed diagnosis or undertreatment risks irreversible intellectual and motor impairment, while some hydrogen peroxide-system defects prove transient and permit later withdrawal of therapy.
pitfalls: Assuming all congenital hypothyroidism is due to dysgenesis and overlooking a heritable biosynthetic defect with recurrence risk.
Missing the sensorineural hearing loss of Pendred syndrome.
Continuing lifelong therapy without re-evaluation in potentially transient DUOX2-related disease.
Providing inadequate replacement that fails to normalise thyroid status during early brain development.
Interpreting a normal-sized gland on imaging as excluding dyshormonogenesis.
references: Newborn screening and congenital hypothyroidism guidance
Clinical genetics reference resources on thyroid disorders
management: Prompt levothyroxine replacement titrated to normalise thyroid function and protect brain development
Monitor TSH and free thyroxine and adjust the dose through growth
Plan later re-evaluation off treatment, as hydrogen-peroxide-system defects (DUOX2, DUOXA2) may prove transient rather than permanent
Audiological assessment and hearing support where Pendred syndrome is identified
Monitor goitre size, since persistent thyroid-stimulating hormone drive causes glandular hyperplasia
Developmental surveillance with continued paediatric endocrinology follow-up
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with sibling recurrence risk and carrier testing
